subject: Quantized latency benchmarking plan — hosted vs incumbent
messages:
From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>
To: Amit Shah <amit.shah@acme-ai.com>, Sara Lopez <sara.lopez@acme-ai.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 01 Dec 2026 15:20:00 -0800
Subject: Recap & next steps — latency targets and POC scope

Hi Amit / Sara,

Thanks again for the call today — good alignment. Short recap and suggested next steps so we can move to a short hosted POC that directly compares end-to-end p95/p99 against your incumbent provider.

What we captured (please correct if I mis-remember):
- Target production SLOs: p95 <= 120ms, p99 <= 320ms (for synchronous text-gen API; streaming considered separately)
- Expected concurrency: bursts to 180 qps, sustained 60 qps during peak window
- Typical request shape: 80% short prompts (~40 tokens total), 20% long prompts (200-800 tokens)
- Streaming requirements: client-side realtime for incremental tokens; target end-to-first-token latency <= 40ms for short prompts
- Incumbent observed tail: you mentioned occasional p99s in the 600-900ms range during peak windows

Attachments I dropped: initial-latency-spec.xlsx (rough SLO table + measurement plan).

Proposed next steps (hosted POC path):
1) You share a redacted sample traffic trace + incumbent tail CSV (or we can accept synthetic shapes) — aim: by Thu 12/3
2) Redwood runs a 48h hosted micro-benchmark against a pinned model variant (we'll mirror the token distribution you share) — target start 12/6
3) We provide: per-token cost estimate, p95/p99 histograms, concurrent throughput chart, and streaming-first-token latency breakdown — report by EOD 12/8
4) Quick sync to review results and decide next phase (dedicated or private) — propose 12/9 10am PT

Open questions I want to confirm:
- Do you need KV-caching/prefix caching behavior during POC, or can we run cold-start only?
- Any regulatory constraints around sample trace storage/retention?

If that plan looks good I'll prepare the hosted POC runbook and a calendar invite for 12/6 start.

Thanks,
Hannah

Thanks Hannah — that summary looks right. Couple clarifications and I attached the incumbent sample CSV.

Clarifications:
- Our current provider reports p95 ~ 180ms during steady load, and p99 spikes to 700-950ms under bursty traffic (incumbent-latency-samples.csv attached).
- We do have a lightweight prefix cache in prod (20% hit rate) but for the POC we are fine running cold-start only to get conservative numbers.
- Retention: please do not store raw traces longer than 7 days; we can provide redacted payloads.

Also attaching a short CSV of production request size distribution. Let me know if you need additional columns (tokens, response size, timestamp buckets).

—Amit

Date: Thu, 03 Dec 2026 11:05:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Recap & next steps — latency targets and POC scope

Amit — thanks for the CSV, that helps a lot. Quick note on the micro-benchmark plan I'm proposing (high level):

Micro-benchmark plan (48h hosted run) — goals: reproduce your token distribution + measure end-to-end p95/p99, throughput at concurrency, and first-token streaming latency
- Workload: synthetic replayer that follows your supplied distribution (short/long split + arrival process).
- Model: we will run against a close open checkpoint (configurable). For quantized runs we'll test q4_0 and q8_0 execution paths.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 total latency, cold vs warmed KV-cache runs, per-concurrency breakdown (1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 180 qps), streaming-first-token latency for short prompts.
- Output: histogram exports (CSV), flamegraph of request latencies, and resource utilization per GPU.

Questions for you to unblock:
- Can you confirm tokenization details (we need an example prompt and the tokenizer name / model family)
- Any request-level headers we should preserve in the replay so we mimic client behavior?

I've put the draft runbook in the shared Drive folder here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3cACME-latency-bench
I'll also prepare a small synthetic workload that you can run against your incumbent to validate the shape before we run hosted.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Amit Shah <amit.shah@acme-ai.com>
Date: Fri, 04 Dec 2026 08:30:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Recap & next steps — latency targets and POC scope

Looping in some implementation constraints from our side so expectations are clear: 

Implementation notes / trade-offs:
- Quantized execution: for the short prompt heavy workload, q4_0 yields ~1.6x throughput improvement and reduces tail compared to fp16 in our internal runs for similar models. We'll include q4_0 and q8_0 runs in the POC.
- Streaming-first-token: achieving <=40ms end-to-first-token is feasible with our streaming fast-path but depends on network hop (we recommend running hosted POC from our us-west region to match your user geography).
- Concurrency shaping: to simulate bursty traffic we recommend 3 phases (ramp to sustained qps -> 10min spike -> cooldown) and repeat across the 48h window to catch warm/cold KV-cache behavior.
- Observability: we'll publish per-request traces (trace ids only) and anonymized latency histograms; raw payloads will be deleted per your 7-day retention request.

Proposed concrete numbers to record in the runbook:
- Warm/cold distinction: run 12h cold baseline, then enable prefix caching with a 20% hit pattern for the next 12h, then run spike experiments.
- Targets to evaluate: p95 <= 120ms (goal), p99 <= 320ms (goal), streaming-first-token <= 40ms. If p99 is > 500ms we consider additional tuning (different model size or routing to dedicated pool).

I'll add these to the POC runbook and coordinate with infra to ensure we pin GPUs and quantization kernels.

Karthik
Karthik Iyer
